title: Lukla flights from Ramechhap in peak season
meta_description: In peak season most Lukla flights leave from Manthali airport in Ramechhap, 4 to 5 hours from Kathmandu. How the night drive, flight and delays work.
summary: In the busy spring and autumn seasons, most flights to Lukla for the Everest region leave from Manthali airport in Ramechhap district, not Kathmandu. That means a drive of about 130 km and 4 to 5 hours, usually leaving at 1 or 2 am, then a 20-minute flight. Keep spare days for weather.
key_takeaways: In recent years most Lukla flights in April, May, October and November have left from Manthali airport in Ramechhap; check current status before you travel.
Ramechhap is about 130 km from Kathmandu, 4 to 5 hours by road, so hotel pick-up is usually at 1 or 2 am.
The flight to Lukla takes about 20 minutes and only runs in clear weather; delays of hours or days are normal.
Pack to 15 kg in total, and keep at least one spare day in Kathmandu after the trek, two in winter or monsoon.

sections.heading: Why the flights moved to Ramechhap
paras: For decades, the Everest trek began at Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport with a flight of about 35 minutes to Lukla. As trekking grew, dozens of small Lukla flights each morning competed for space with international and other domestic traffic on Kathmandu's single runway. From 2019 the authorities began moving most Lukla flights in the peak seasons to Manthali airport in Ramechhap district, south-east of Kathmandu.

In recent years this has applied roughly from April to May and from October to November, and in some years for longer. Outside those months, many flights still leave from Kathmandu. The arrangement is decided each season by the civil aviation authorities and the airlines, so check current status before you travel. We confirm which airport your flight uses when we book the tickets, and plan the transfer around it.

sections.heading: A peak-season morning, hour by hour
paras: Lukla flights leave at first light, because mornings have the clearest air and cloud builds up the valleys by late morning. From Ramechhap, that means a night drive. The table shows a typical morning in October, as we see it most weeks of the season. Times shift with sunrise and with the airline's slot.

sections.heading: The runway at the other end
paras: Lukla's airstrip was built in 1964 by Edmund Hillary and the Sherpas he worked with, to bring in materials for the schools and clinics of the Himalayan Trust. It was renamed Tenzing-Hillary Airport in 2008. The runway is about 527 m long and slopes at roughly 12 percent, uphill for landing and downhill for take-off. One end stops at the mountainside and the other drops to the valley.

Only small short-take-off aircraft use it, mostly Twin Otters, Dornier 228s and Let L-410s with about 14 to 19 seats. Pilots fly by sight, which is why weather matters more than anything else. Cloud at Lukla, at Ramechhap or over the ridges in between stops flights, even when the sky above you looks clear. Each aircraft flies several rotations a morning, so a two-hour delay to the first flight pushes every later flight back too.
On the way in, sit on the left side of the aircraft for the mountains to the north; on the way back, sit on the right.

sections.heading: Baggage, waiting and what to carry
paras: The usual baggage allowance is 15 kg per person in total, normally about 10 kg checked and 5 kg in hand. Extra weight is charged per kilo if there is room, and in busy weeks it may go on a later flight. Leave everything you do not need on the trek at your Kathmandu hotel; every trekking hotel stores bags for free.

Manthali is a small airport. There is a waiting hall that is crowded in peak weeks, simple toilets and a few tea stalls outside. On a bad weather morning you may wait there for several hours, and sometimes flights are cancelled for the day and you drive back or stay nearby. Bring what makes waiting bearable.
list: A warm layer and a hat for the pre-dawn wait, which can be cold even in October.
Water, snacks and the packed breakfast the hotel gives you.
Passport, permits and medicines in your hand luggage, never in the porter duffel.
A book or downloaded films; mobile data at the airport is slow when the hall is full.
Patience: no one can make the cloud at Lukla lift, and pressure on pilots is the last thing anyone wants.

sections.heading: The flight back out
paras: Most trekkers worry about the flight in, but the flight out is the one that decides whether you make your connection home. Your guide confirms your seat with the airline office in Lukla the afternoon before, and you are usually told the evening before which rotation you are on. Early rotations are the safest, because cloud tends to build through the morning.

On the morning itself, you walk a few minutes from the lodge to the terminal, check in, have bags weighed again and wait in a small hall above the runway. When the first aircraft from Ramechhap or Kathmandu appears over the ridge, the hall goes quiet. Planes turn round in a few minutes, so be at the gate when your name is called.

If the flight lands at Ramechhap, a car is waiting for the 4 to 5 hour drive back to Kathmandu, and you are usually at your hotel by early afternoon. If cloud closes Lukla for the day, you stay another night in the same lodge and go on the first flights the next morning. Lodges in Lukla are used to this.

sections.heading: Spare days and the walk-in option
paras: Our rule is the same in every season: at least one spare day in Kathmandu after the trek, and two from December to February and from June to September. On the way in, a day's delay can be absorbed by shortening the trek or using a rest day. On the way out there is no shortcut except a helicopter, and an international flight the day after landing from Lukla is a gamble. If the spare day is not needed, it becomes a free day for Patan or Boudhanath.

When flights are cancelled for a day or more, helicopter operators sell shared seats between Lukla and Ramechhap or Kathmandu. A shared seat has typically cost several hundred US dollars per person in recent seasons, more when demand is high. Policies that cover trekking usually pay for a helicopter in a medical emergency, but often not for weather delays alone. Read your policy before you leave home.

You can avoid the flight in altogether. From Phaplu or Salleri in Solu, reached by road in about 9 to 11 hours from Kathmandu, the old trail through Junbesi, Nunthala and Kharikhola reaches Lukla in five to six days. The walk acclimatises you naturally, passes Sherpa and Rai villages that most trekkers fly over, and leaves only the flight out to plan around.

sections.heading: Permits on landing
paras: Before you leave Lukla on foot, your guide shows or buys the local municipality permit, which the Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality charges every foreign trekker. The Sagarmatha National Park entry permit is checked at Monjo, below Namche Bazaar. Since April 2023 Nepal requires foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas to trek with a licensed guide; in the Khumbu, where the local municipality runs its own permit, the rule has been applied unevenly. We trek with licensed guides on every route. Check current status before you travel.

The trail itself starts at the stone arch at the top of Lukla's main street. From there it is about 3 to 4 hours to Phakding, and the next day you climb to Namche Bazaar at 3,440 m, where the first acclimatisation day of almost every Everest trek is spent.

faqs.q: Do Lukla flights leave from Kathmandu or Ramechhap?
faqs.a: It depends on the season. In recent years most Lukla flights in the peak months of April, May, October and November have left from Manthali airport in Ramechhap, while many flights in the quieter months still leave from Kathmandu. The arrangement is set each season by the aviation authorities and airlines, so check current status before you travel and confirm the airport on your ticket.

faqs.q: How far is Ramechhap from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Manthali airport in Ramechhap is about 130 km from Kathmandu, a drive of 4 to 5 hours on a winding road. Because Lukla flights leave at first light, pick-up from a Kathmandu hotel is usually at 1 or 2 am. On the way back you land at Ramechhap in the morning and reach Kathmandu in the early afternoon if the road is clear.

faqs.q: How often are Lukla flights delayed?
faqs.a: Often enough that every plan should allow for it. Flights only run in clear weather, and cloud at Lukla, at the departure airport or on the route stops them. Delays of a few hours are common in any season; cancellations for a day or more are most common from June to September and on winter mornings. Keep one or two spare days after the trek.

faqs.q: What is the baggage limit on Lukla flights?
faqs.a: The usual allowance is 15 kg per person in total, normally split as about 10 kg checked and 5 kg hand luggage. Extra weight is charged per kilo if there is space, and in peak weeks excess bags may follow on a later flight. Pack the porter duffel to 10 kg and leave the rest at your Kathmandu hotel, which will store it for free.

faqs.q: Can I avoid the Lukla flight?
faqs.a: Yes. You can drive to Phaplu or Salleri in Solu, about 9 to 11 hours from Kathmandu, and walk the old trail through Junbesi, Nunthala and Kharikhola to Lukla in five to six days. It acclimatises you well and passes quiet villages. You can then fly out from Lukla, or walk back the same way if you have time.

cta.text: We book the flight, the night transfer to Ramechhap and the spare days, and keep watching the weather while you sleep.
